Will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric kettle? (US 120 V)

Tight fit — no usable-capacity figure see why below ↓

Inside the rated output, past the design line. 1,500 W against 1,800 W continuous — 83% of it, past the 82% line this site drops out of the green at. It will run, with nothing left for a hot day or a second appliance.

Official spec + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-16 · US 120 V unit × electric kettle

Nominal capacity 1,024 Wh
Surge headroom 2.4×

Running1,500 Wof1,800 Wcontinuous output

0 – 1,800 W across the rails above

No start-up rail: this load has no locked rotor to publish an inrush for, so no start-up demand was checked.

Two numbers decide this, and readers use them interchangeably: watts are the ceiling on what the inverter holds at any instant, watt-hours are how much energy the battery holds. A machine can have plenty of one and not enough of the other.

The verdict is a calculation, not a lookup. What it will not do is print a runtime, and the reason is specific: we read 3 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-08 and found no depth of discharge or inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them, so there is no usable-capacity figure to divide.

Where those numbers come from

A blank is never left blank. A field we have found no figure for says so, and a field whose sources disagree — two documents, or one document with itself — says that instead of picking one.

No usable-capacity figure for this machine

EcoFlow states a nameplate watt-hour number for it, and we read 3 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-08 and found no depth of discharge or inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them. Dividing the nameplate by this load would be wrong by 20–35% in the flattering direction, so this page shows the nameplate for what it is and refuses to turn it into hours.

Missing: station.usable_capacity_wh

Energy rate instead of a runtime

1,500 Wh per hour averaged over this load’s duty cycle

This number needs no battery figure at all, which is why this page can give it when it cannot give hours. Divide any usable-capacity figure you trust by it and you have your own runtime, with our arithmetic visible instead of hidden.

Questions people ask about this pairing

Will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric kettle?
Yes, but with very little room. 1,500 W of running draw against 1,800 W of continuous output — 83% of it. Anything past 82% of continuous output drops out of the green on this site, because a rating is a ceiling and a hot afternoon is not a laboratory. The verdict is computed from running watts, and inverter waveform — the working is in the evidence section above.
How long will an EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus run an electric kettle?
We will not put a number on it, and that is a finding rather than a gap. We read 3 of EcoFlow’s own published documents on 2026-08-08 and found no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency for the US 120 V build in them. What it does state is a nameplate watt-hour rating. Dividing that nameplate by this load produces a figure that is typically 20–35% too high while looking exactly as authoritative as a real one. What this page gives instead is the load's energy rate in watt-hours per hour, which needs no battery figure at all.
Why is this amber when the watts fit?
Because 83% of a continuous rating is not headroom. Above 82% this site drops out of the green: an inverter's rating is measured under conditions your kitchen is not, a warm machine derates, and the moment a second appliance joins the circuit the margin is gone. It will run. We are declining to call it comfortable.
